scenes.title: Character and Emotion in Judgment
scenes.summary: Since rhetoric aims at judgment, the speaker must not only make his argument demonstrative but also show himself of a certain character and put the judge in a certain frame of mind: character counts most in advice, the hearer's state in the courts, for things do not look the same to those who love and those who hate, to the angry and the calm.

scenes.title: Practical Wisdom, Virtue and Goodwill
scenes.summary: Speakers are credible through three things, practical wisdom, virtue and goodwill, since men speak falsely through folly, depravity or ill will; the first two are to be had from the account of the virtues, goodwill and friendship from that of the emotions.

scenes.title: The Emotions
scenes.summary: The emotions are what change people's judgments and are attended by pain and pleasure, such as anger, pity and fear; each is to be treated under three heads: the state in which people feel it, the people toward whom they feel it, and its grounds.
